----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the API documentation for the content_types library.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Forward lookup

Map a filename, bare extension, Path, or URL to its MIME / content type.


get_content_type(filename_or_extension: str | pathlib.Path, treat_as_binary: bool = True, fallback: str | None | content_types._Unset = _UNSET) -> str | None

Return the most specific, commonly accepted MIME type for a filename or extension.

The lookup is based purely on the extension — the file's bytes are never read. A
filename, a bare extension (with or without a leading dot), or a `pathlib.Path` are
all accepted. For URLs, any query string (`?...`) or fragment (`#...`) is stripped
first; for compound extensions the last segment wins (`archive.tar.gz` resolves as
`gz`). Matching is case-insensitive.

Args:
    filename_or_extension: A filename, path, URL, or bare extension to look up.
        Accepts a `str` or a `pathlib.Path`.
    treat_as_binary: Selects the default fallback when the extension is unknown and
        no explicit `fallback` is given. `True` (default) returns
        `application/octet-stream`; `False` returns `text/plain`.
    fallback: An explicit value to return for unknown extensions. When provided, it
        takes precedence over `treat_as_binary`. Pass a MIME type string to override
        the default, or `None` to get `None` back for unknowns (handy when you want to
        branch on a miss rather than receive a placeholder type). When omitted entirely,
        the `treat_as_binary` default is used — so existing callers are unaffected.

Returns:
    For a known extension, its MIME type; otherwise the explicit `fallback` (which may be `None`) or the default.

Raises:
    TypeError: If `filename_or_extension` is `None`.

Example:
    ```python
    >>> get_content_type("picture.jpg")
    'image/jpeg'
    >>> get_content_type(".webp")
    'image/webp'
    >>> get_content_type("script.js")
    'text/javascript'
    >>> get_content_type("unknown.xyz")
    'application/octet-stream'
    >>> get_content_type("unknown.xyz", treat_as_binary=False)
    'text/plain'
    >>> get_content_type("unknown.xyz", fallback='application/x-custom')
    'application/x-custom'
    >>> get_content_type("unknown.xyz", fallback=None) is None
    True
    ```


## Reverse lookup

Map a MIME / content type back to its file extension(s) — the inverse of get_content_type.


guess_extension(content_type: str, with_dot: bool = True) -> str | None

Return the canonical file extension for a MIME / content type.

This is the reverse of get_content_type(). The lookup is case-insensitive and any
MIME parameters are ignored, so an HTTP `Content-Type` header value such as
`text/html; charset=utf-8` resolves the same as `text/html`. Common non-canonical
or legacy spellings are also accepted — `text/json` resolves like `application/json`
and `image/jpg` like `image/jpeg`. When a content type maps to several extensions,
the canonical one is returned (e.g. `image/jpeg` -> `.jpg`); use
guess_all_extensions() to get every extension.

The canonical choice follows this library's table and may differ from the standard
library `mimetypes` module — for example, this returns `.html` for `text/html`.

Args:
    content_type: A MIME type to look up, optionally with parameters
        (e.g. `application/pdf` or `text/html; charset=utf-8`).
    with_dot: When `True` (default) the returned extension has a leading dot
        (e.g. `.pdf`), which is what you concatenate onto a filename. When `False`
        the bare extension is returned (e.g. `pdf`).

Returns:
    The canonical extension for the content type, or `None` if it is unknown
    (including empty, whitespace-only, or parameter-only input).

Raises:
    TypeError: If `content_type` is `None`.

Example:
    ```python
    >>> guess_extension("application/pdf")
    '.pdf'
    >>> guess_extension("image/jpeg")
    '.jpg'
    >>> guess_extension("text/html; charset=utf-8")
    '.html'
    >>> guess_extension("application/pdf", with_dot=False)
    'pdf'
    >>> guess_extension("application/x-does-not-exist") is None
    True
    ```

guess_all_extensions(content_type: str, with_dot: bool = True) -> list[str]

Return every known file extension for a MIME / content type, canonical first.

Like guess_extension(), but returns the full list rather than just the canonical
extension. The lookup is case-insensitive, MIME parameters are ignored, and common
non-canonical spellings (e.g. `text/json`, `image/jpg`) resolve to their canonical
type. The first element always equals guess_extension(content_type). The order
follows this library's table (canonical first) and is not guaranteed to match the
standard library `mimetypes` module.

Args:
    content_type: A MIME type to look up, optionally with parameters
        (e.g. `image/jpeg` or `text/html; charset=utf-8`).
    with_dot: When `True` (default) each extension has a leading dot (e.g. `.jpg`);
        when `False` the bare extensions are returned (e.g. `jpg`).

Returns:
    A list of extensions, canonical first, or an empty list if the content type is
    unknown (including empty, whitespace-only, or parameter-only input).

Raises:
    TypeError: If `content_type` is `None`.

Example:
    ```python
    >>> guess_all_extensions("image/jpeg")
    ['.jpg', '.jpeg', '.jpe']
    >>> guess_all_extensions("text/html")
    ['.html', '.htm']
    >>> guess_all_extensions("application/pdf")
    ['.pdf']
    >>> guess_all_extensions("application/x-does-not-exist")
    []
    ```


## Mapping data

The underlying extension -> content-type table (364 entries; keys have no leading dot).


EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE

dict() -> new empty dictionary
dict(mapping) -> new dictionary initialized from a mapping object's
    (key, value) pairs
dict(iterable) -> new dictionary initialized as if via:
    d = {}
    for k, v in iterable:
        d[k] = v
dict(**kwargs) -> new dictionary initialized with the name=value pairs
    in the keyword argument list.  For example:  dict(one=1, two=2)

----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the User Guide documentation for the package.
----------------------------------------------------------------------

### Getting started

Imagine someone hands you a sealed envelope and asks what is inside. You are not allowed to open it. All you get is the label on the front. That is the job content-types does, and it turns out the label is usually enough.

## The envelope problem

Here is how the problem shows up in real code. You have a bucket in S3 with a few hundred thousand objects. A customer's browser asks for one of them, and your job is to send back a `Content-Type` header so the browser knows whether to render an image, play audio, or offer a download. The honest way to find out is to fetch the object and look at its first few bytes. The honest way is also slow, costs money, and is silly when the key already says `invoice-2026-03.pdf`.

The same situation shows up when you are uploading. S3 will happily store `report.pdf` as `binary/octet-stream` if you let it, and then every link to that file becomes a download instead of a tab. You want to set the type correctly at upload time, and again, you already know the filename.

content-types answers the question from the label. It takes the extension, looks it up in a table of 364 entries, and returns the type. It never opens, reads, or sniffs anything, so it is safe to call on names of files that live on another machine, on URLs you have not fetched, and on files that do not exist yet.

## Install

Requires Python 3.10 or later. There are no runtime dependencies, so it adds nothing to your lock file but itself.

```bash
uv add content-types
# or
pip install content-types
```

## The first lookup

```python
import content_types

content_types.get_content_type('report.pdf')
# 'application/pdf'
```

That is the whole core API. One function, one string in, one string out. The import name is `content_types` with an underscore; the distribution and the command line tool are `content-types` with a hyphen. Python cannot import a hyphen, so the two spellings are a fact of life.

## It is not fussy about what you hand it

The function was written by someone who got tired of normalising filenames before every call, so it does the normalising for you. A full path, a bare extension with or without the dot, a `pathlib.Path`, or a URL all work, and case does not matter.

```python
from pathlib import Path

content_types.get_content_type('photo.JPG')  # 'image/jpeg'
content_types.get_content_type('images/photo.jpg')  # 'image/jpeg'
content_types.get_content_type('jpg')  # 'image/jpeg'
content_types.get_content_type('.jpg')  # 'image/jpeg'
content_types.get_content_type(Path('/data/photo.jpg'))  # 'image/jpeg'
content_types.get_content_type('https://cdn.example.com/a.mp3?v=3#t=10')  # 'audio/mpeg'
```

Three details are worth knowing up front, because each one has surprised someone.

- For URLs, the query string and the fragment are thrown away before the lookup. A cache-busting `?v=3` does not turn your MP3 into a mystery.
- For compound extensions the last segment wins. `archive.tar.gz` resolves as `gz` and returns `application/gzip`, which is the right answer for the outer container. There is no special knowledge of `.tar.gz` as a unit.
- Dotfiles such as `.env` and `.gitignore` are in the table and resolve to `text/plain`. They are extensions with no name in front, and the lookup treats them that way.

## When the label is blank

Sometimes the envelope says `Makefile`, or `notes.xyz`, or nothing at all. For those the function returns `application/octet-stream`, the universal "it is bytes, I cannot tell you more" type. That is the correct thing to put in a header, but it is not always what you want in your own logic, and it hides the fact that a lookup missed. The next page, [Unknown extensions](unknown-extensions.qmd), is about telling a miss from a hit and deciding what to do about it.

## Shortcut constants

For a handful of formats you reach for daily, the module hands you the answer as a plain string so you do not even write the call.

```python
content_types.json  # 'application/json'
content_types.pdf  # 'application/pdf'
content_types.parquet  # 'application/vnd.apache.parquet'
```

The full set is `webp`, `png`, `jpg`, `mp3`, `json`, `pdf`, `zip`, `xml`, `csv`, `md`, `parquet`, `ipynb`, `pkl`, `yaml`, `toml`, and `sqlite`. One caution: write `import content_types` and use attribute access. `from content_types import json` quietly shadows the standard library `json` module, and you will spend an unhappy afternoon wondering why `json.loads` is a string.

## Where to go next

- [Unknown extensions](unknown-extensions.qmd) is the detective work: telling a miss from a hit and the three ways to handle one.
- [Reverse lookup](reverse-lookup.qmd) runs the envelope backwards, from a content type or a `Content-Type` header to an extension.
- [Command line](cli.qmd) covers the `content-types` tool for quick answers in a shell.
- [Compared to mimetypes](compared-to-mimetypes.qmd) explains why the standard library was not enough and how the table differs.
- [FAQ](faq.qmd) collects the questions people actually ask.
- The [API reference](../reference/index.qmd) lists every public name with its signature.


### Unknown extensions

Every lookup returns something. That is convenient right up to the moment you need to know whether the answer was a confident match or a shrug. This page is about telling the two apart, and about what to do once you can.

## The shrug looks like an answer

`get_content_type()` returns a string unless you ask it not to. For a known extension the string is the content type. For an unknown one it is a fallback, and the default fallback is `application/octet-stream`.

```python
import content_types

content_types.get_content_type('data.parquet')  # 'application/vnd.apache.parquet'
content_types.get_content_type('notes.xyz')  # 'application/octet-stream'
content_types.get_content_type('Makefile')  # 'application/octet-stream'
```

`application/octet-stream` is a perfectly good header. It is what S3 and most web servers send when they do not know better, and browsers respond by offering a download, which is the safe move for mystery bytes. The trouble is that it is also a real answer. A handful of formats genuinely map to it, on purpose, because there is no better registered type: `.bin`, `.pkl`, `.npy`, `.so`, `.o`, and a few more. So when you see `application/octet-stream` come back, you cannot tell from the string alone whether the table recognised the extension or gave up.

Think of it as a detective who, when stumped, writes "unknown substance" on the report. Useful, as long as you remember that some substances really are labelled "unknown substance".

## Three ways to handle a miss

**Change the shrug.** If the files you deal with are mostly text, tell the lookup to shrug in the other direction. `treat_as_binary=False` swaps the default fallback for `text/plain`.

```python
content_types.get_content_type('notes.xyz', treat_as_binary=False)  # 'text/plain'
```

**Write your own shrug.** Pass any string as `fallback` and that is what comes back for every unknown extension. It outranks `treat_as_binary`. Known extensions are untouched.

```python
content_types.get_content_type('notes.xyz', fallback='application/x-acme')  # 'application/x-acme'
content_types.get_content_type('photo.jpg', fallback='application/x-acme')  # 'image/jpeg'
```

**Refuse to shrug.** Pass `fallback=None` and a miss comes back as `None`. Now you can branch. This is the mode to use when a miss should change what the program does next, for example to hand the file to a byte-sniffing library, to reject the upload, or to log it for a human.

```python
content_type = content_types.get_content_type(name, fallback=None)
if content_type is None:
    content_type = sniff_with_python_magic(path)
```

One subtlety that bites people who skim: leaving `fallback` out and passing `fallback=None` are different things. Leaving it out keeps the historical default. The parameter's real default is a private sentinel, precisely so that an explicit `None` can mean "give me `None`" without changing behaviour for every caller who never passes the argument. Your type checker knows this too. The plain call types as `str`, and only `fallback=None` widens it to `Optional[str]`.

## Ask the table directly

If you only want a yes or a no, skip the function and ask the table. Keys are bare lowercase extensions with no leading dot.

```python
ext = 'parquet'
ext in content_types.EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE  # True
```

## Teaching it a new word

The table is a plain `dict`, and the forward lookup reads it fresh on every call, so an addition takes effect immediately. Keys must be lowercase and have no leading dot.

```python
content_types.EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE['acme'] = 'application/x-acme'
content_types.get_content_type('report.acme')  # 'application/x-acme'
```

Do this once at startup, not inside a request handler. And do it before the first reverse lookup, because `guess_extension()` builds its inverted view of the table on first use and caches it for the life of the process. Additions made after that are visible to the forward lookup but invisible to the reverse one.

If the extension is a real, widely used format that other people would reasonably expect to work, do not keep the fix to yourself. [Open an issue](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/content-types/issues) or send a pull request and it ends up in the table for everyone.

## Things that look like misses but are not

- `None` as the filename raises `TypeError`. That is a bug in the caller, not an unknown extension, and the library refuses to paper over it.
- `archive.tar.gz` returns `application/gzip`. That is a hit on the last segment, and it is the correct type for the compressed container.

And things that are misses, in case you were wondering: an empty string, a name with no dot anywhere, and a URL with no file component such as `https://example.com/download`. All three get the fallback.


### Reverse lookup

So far the envelope has had a label and you wanted to know what was inside. Now flip it. A server has just told you what is inside, in the form of a `Content-Type` header, and you need to write a label. That is reverse lookup, and it is harder than it sounds.

## From a type to an extension

`guess_extension()` is the inverse of `get_content_type()`. Give it a content type and it returns the canonical extension, with the dot, ready to append to a filename. `guess_all_extensions()` returns every extension known for that type, canonical first.

```python
import content_types

content_types.guess_extension('application/pdf')  # '.pdf'
content_types.guess_extension('image/jpeg')  # '.jpg'
content_types.guess_all_extensions('image/jpeg')  # ['.jpg', '.jpeg', '.jpe']
content_types.guess_extension('image/jpeg', with_dot=False)  # 'jpg'
```

The classic use is naming a download when the URL gives you nothing to go on.

```python
import httpx
from pathlib import Path

resp = httpx.get('https://example.com/download/item')
ext = content_types.guess_extension(resp.headers['content-type'])
if ext:
    Path(f'downloaded{ext}').write_bytes(resp.content)
```

## Why the reverse direction is the hard one

The forward table is one-to-one. Each of its 364 extensions maps to exactly one type. Run it backwards and it is one-to-many: those 364 extensions collapse onto 223 types, and 57 of those types have more than one extension pointing at them. `image/jpeg` is claimed by `.jpg`, `.jpeg`, and `.jpe`. Which one do you write on the label? Someone has to pick, and the pick has to be stable.

The rule is that the first extension listed for a type in `EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE` wins, with a short list of deliberate overrides where the first-listed spelling is the one nobody uses any more: `text/html` gives `.html` not `.htm`, `image/tiff` gives `.tiff`, `video/mpeg` gives `.mpeg`, and `application/x-msdownload` gives `.exe` rather than `.dll`. Whatever the pick, `guess_extension(t)` is always equal to `guess_all_extensions(t)[0]`, and a test enforces it.

The standard library makes its own picks and orders its lists differently, so do not expect the two to agree. [Compared to mimetypes](compared-to-mimetypes.qmd) has the details.

## It reads headers as servers actually write them

Real `Content-Type` headers are messy. They carry parameters, they vary in case, and a surprising number of servers send spellings that were never registered. The reverse lookup takes all of that in stride.

- Case is ignored. `IMAGE/JPEG` resolves like `image/jpeg`.
- Parameters are stripped, so you can pass the raw header value. `text/html; charset=utf-8` resolves like `text/html`.
- Legacy and mistaken spellings resolve to the type this library uses. `text/json`, `image/jpg`, `audio/mp3`, `text/xml`, `application/javascript`, `application/x-yaml`, `application/x-zip-compressed`, and `application/x-gzip` all work. The complete alias list lives in the source as `_CONTENT_TYPE_ALIASES`, and tests check that every alias points at a real type and never shadows one.

## When it does not know

An unknown content type is not an error. `guess_extension()` returns `None` and `guess_all_extensions()` returns `[]`. Empty, whitespace-only, and parameter-only input all count as unknown. Passing `None` raises `TypeError`, matching the forward function.

```python
content_types.guess_extension('application/x-nope')  # None
content_types.guess_all_extensions('application/x-nope')  # []
```

The `or` idiom is your friend here: `guess_extension(header) or '.bin'` gives you a usable label every time.

## The two catch-all types

`text/plain` and `application/octet-stream` are where extensions go when nothing more specific exists. `text/plain` has 32 extensions in the table and `application/octet-stream` has 24. Asked for the canonical pick, the library gives you `.txt` and `.bin`, which is as sensible as it gets. Asked for the full list, it gives you config files, pickles, object files, and database fragments all in one pile. If a server tells you `application/octet-stream`, the honest reading is that it does not know either, and any extension you write is a guess.


### Command line

Sometimes the question is not in your code at all. You are staring at a bucket listing, or a log line, or a colleague's message, and you want to know what `report.parq` is going to be served as without opening a REPL. The package ships a small console script for exactly that moment.

## Install

Install it as a tool so it is on your path everywhere.

```bash
uv tool install content-types
# or
pipx install content-types
```

Inside a project that already depends on the package the script is on the virtualenv's path, so `uv run content-types ...` works there without a separate install.

## Use

One argument in, one line out.

```bash
content-types example.jpg
# image/jpeg

content-types .webp
# image/webp

content-types data.parquet
# application/vnd.apache.parquet
```

The argument goes straight through `get_content_type()` with its defaults, so the tool inherits the library's manners: case does not matter, a bare extension works with or without the dot, and an unknown extension prints `application/octet-stream` and exits 0. It does the forward lookup only. For the reverse direction, open Python.

## Flags and exit codes

The script is deliberately tiny, so this table is the whole contract.

| Invocation | Output | Exit code |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `content-types NAME` | the content type, or `application/octet-stream` for an unknown extension | 0 |
| `content-types` | usage text on stdout | 1 |
| `content-types -h` or `--help` | usage text | 0 |
| `content-types --version` | the installed package version | 0 |

Extra arguments after the first are ignored. There are no environment variables and no configuration file to discover. Under the hood the script is the function `content_types.cli()` wired up in `pyproject.toml`, which means you can call it yourself if you ever want the same behaviour from inside another tool.


### Compared to mimetypes

Python already ships a `mimetypes` module, and the first question anyone sensible asks is why this library exists at all. The short answer is that `mimetypes` was tried first and came up short in two different ways. The longer answer is this page.

## How the lookup works

There is no magic to describe, and that is the point. Everything is one dictionary, `EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE`, with 364 bare lowercase extensions as keys. `get_content_type()` trims its input down to the last dot-separated segment, lowercases it, and reads the dictionary. The reverse functions invert that same dictionary the first time they are called and cache the result for the life of the process. Nothing is read from disk, no system `mime.types` file is consulted, and the answers are identical on every operating system and every Python version. Same input, same output, forever.

## The two problems with the standard library

**It depends on which Python you are running.** The built-in table in `mimetypes` has 142 entries on Python 3.10. By Python 3.15 it has grown to about 210. That growth is good news, but it means the answer to "what type is `.yaml`" changes with your interpreter: on 3.15 the standard library knows, and on 3.12 it returns `None`. Between 170 and 220 of this library's extensions are missing from `mimetypes`, depending on the version. Some are missing on every supported Python: `.tgz`, `.parquet`, `.ipynb`, `.rs`, `.go`, `.tsx`, `.psd`, and `.dwg` among them. Others, such as `.yaml`, `.toml`, `.webp`, `.flac`, `.epub`, and `.mkv`, were added in recent releases, so code that works on a developer's laptop can fail quietly on an older production image.

**Some of its answers are out of date.** `mimetypes` still returns `text/xml` for `.xml`, where [MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/MIME_types/Common_types) and current practice say `application/xml`. This library standardises on the modern type and keeps the old spelling as an alias on reverse lookup, so you are never stranded by a server that sends the legacy form. The other deliberate choices follow the same logic: `.js` is `text/javascript`, `.yaml` and `.yml` are `application/yaml` per RFC 9512, and `.md` is `text/markdown`.

## The API is not the same either

Do not guess this library's API from the standard library's. `get_content_type()` returns one string, not the `(type, encoding)` tuple that `mimetypes.guess_type()` returns, and it never hands you `None` unless you ask for that with `fallback=None`. The reverse functions keep the familiar names, `guess_extension()` and `guess_all_extensions()`, but they accept raw header values with parameters, resolve legacy aliases, and can choose a different canonical extension, for example `.html` for `text/html` where the standard library often says `.htm`.

If you want to see the exact differences on your own interpreter rather than take this page's word for it, the repository includes a script that prints them.

```bash
uv run python samples/compare_to_builtin.py
```

## Why not python-magic

`python-magic` and its relatives identify a file by reading its leading bytes. When you have the bytes, that is the more reliable method, and it is the only method that works when the extension is missing or lying. This library exists for the other case: you know the name but not the contents. An object key in S3, a URL you have not fetched, a filename in a form submission. The two are not rivals. `fallback=None` is the hook for handing a miss over to byte sniffing, as shown in [Unknown extensions](unknown-extensions.qmd).

## What is in the table

The 364 entries cover more ground than you would expect from a MIME table. Images including a dozen camera RAW formats. Audio and video from MP3 to DSD to Matroska. Archives and the newer compression formats such as zstd and brotli. Office and OpenDocument files. Source code for around thirty languages. Data science formats such as Parquet, Arrow, HDF5, pickle, NumPy, R, Stata, SAS, and SPSS. Configuration and infrastructure files, Adobe and CAD formats, game engine assets, scientific formats such as FITS, DICOM, and NIfTI, and subtitle files. The [reference page](../reference/EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE.qmd) lists every one.


### FAQ

The questions that actually get asked, with short answers and a pointer to the page that goes deeper.

## Does it read the file?

No, never. Every function works from the name alone. The file does not have to exist, and nothing is opened. If you need byte-level detection, use a sniffing library and fall through to it on a miss as shown in [Unknown extensions](unknown-extensions.qmd).

## Why did I get `application/octet-stream`?

One of two reasons. Either the extension is not in the table, or it is one of the formats that honestly map to that type, such as `.bin`, `.pkl`, or `.npy`. To tell them apart, pass `fallback=None`: a real entry still returns the string, and a miss returns `None`.

## Is `.tar.gz` handled as a unit?

No. The last segment wins, so `archive.tar.gz` returns `application/gzip`, which is the correct type for the compressed container you are actually holding. There is no special casing for double extensions.

## Does it care about case?

No. Extensions are lowercased before the lookup, and content types are lowercased in the reverse direction. `PHOTO.JPG` and `IMAGE/JPEG` both work.

## Does it handle URLs?

Yes. Query strings and fragments are stripped before the lookup, so `https://cdn.example.com/a.mp3?v=3` returns `audio/mpeg`. A URL with no file component, such as `https://example.com/download`, is a miss.

## Why do my `Path` and string results disagree for dotfiles?

They should not. Both `Path('.env')` and the string `'.env'` return `text/plain`. Releases before the next one used `Path.suffix`, which is empty for a dotfile, so the `Path` form quietly fell through to the fallback. That is fixed.

## The type checker says `get_content_type()` returns `Optional[str]`

It returns `str` unless you pass `fallback=None`. The function is overloaded so that the default call and a string `fallback` type as `str`, and only an explicit `fallback=None` types as `Optional[str]`. If your checker still shows the wider type everywhere, you are on a release before the next one.

## Can I add or override an extension?

Yes. Assign into `content_types.EXTENSION_TO_CONTENT_TYPE` with a bare lowercase key. Do it at startup and before the first reverse lookup, because the reverse map is built once and cached. For formats other people would expect to work, open an issue so the table is fixed for everyone.

## Why does `guess_extension('text/html')` return `.html` and not `.htm`?

Because `.html` is what people write today, and `.htm` is a leftover from eight-character filenames. The library keeps a short list of canonical overrides for cases like this. The standard library makes different choices, so do not expect the two to agree.

## What about `text/yaml` or `application/x-yaml`?

The forward direction returns `application/yaml` for `.yaml` and `.yml`, following RFC 9512. The reverse direction accepts the legacy spellings as aliases and returns `.yaml`.

## Is it thread-safe?

Yes for reads, which is all most programs do. The forward lookup is a dictionary read and the reverse map is built with `functools.cache`. If you mutate the table, do it at startup before spawning threads.

## How do I run the tests?

```bash
uv run --with pytest pytest
```

See the [README](https://github.com/mikeckennedy/content-types#development) for lint and docs commands.
